The admin slice is mostly sound, and I want to state that plainly because the risk here is an over-correction pass. Where the slice does break, it breaks in three recognisable patterns rather than randomly:

1. Number-relabelling, not number-invention. The wrong claims almost always contain a real Salesforce number attached to the wrong dimension. Historical Trending's "8" is the Classic per-object trackable-field count re-labelled as snapshot dates (real limit: 5). The report export "2,000" is the on-screen display cap re-labelled as an export cap (real: 100,000). Formula's 3,900 (source characters) and 5,000 (compiled bytes) get merged into a single fictional "compile limit that varies by object". 2. The precision number: of 41 claims I verified against official docs, 23 were CORRECT. Several of the most load-bearing and most-repeated claims in the slice are exactly right, including ones I initially suspected. Bulk API 2.0 is impressively accurate — the 150,000,000-records/24h daily cap, 150 MB after base64, one internal batch per 10,000 records, the 5-minute batch limit with 20 retries before the job moves to Failed, the 100,000-character multipart job creation that auto-transitions to UploadComplete, the >2,000-record crossover, the mandatory UploadComplete PATCH, and the JobComplete-is-not-success model all match the Bulk API 2.0 Developer Guide verbatim. First, the corpus contradicts itself on the two facts it gets wrong most: replay-ID semantics and platform event retention. change-data-capture-integration and platform-events-integration both state -1=tip/-2=earliest correctly while streaming-api-and-pushtopic states it backwards; platform-event-schema-evolution states the 72h/high-volume mapping correctly while platform-events-integration and platform-event-publish-patterns invert it. Templates and scripts/ are amplifiers; a fabrication that reaches them stops being a documentation error and becomes a generator of new documentation errors. slices.claims_checked: Extracted ~95 candidate claims via grep triage (SCREAMING_CASE identifiers, Apex API calls, SOQL FROM targets, numeric limits, permission names, release-version claims, crypto/encoding code fences). Verified 44 distinct claims against official Salesforce documentation (help.salesforce.com articles rendered via the /apex/HTViewHelpDoc path, developer.salesforce.com atlas pages, and official-help quotes surfaced through search where the page would not render). 17 defects found, 20 claims confirmed CORRECT, 1 genuinely UNVERIFIABLE.
slices.health:
Mixed, with a clear pattern: the numbers are trustworthy and the mechanisms are not.

Of 44 claims verified, 20 came back clean and several of those were exactly the claims most likely to have drifted — the June/July 2026 MFA and phishing-resistant-MFA enforcement dates with their four-permission trigger set, the 20/60-field and 18-month/10-year Field Audit Trail limits (including the checker-script constants), the 25-concurrent-long-running-request and 150M-record Bulk 2.0 ceilings, the v46.0 data-classification floor, the 120-second reCAPTCHA token, the LoginHistory-6-months / SetupAuditTrail-180-days forensic table, and the full Auth.SessionManagement method surface. Quantitative and enumerated content in this slice is in good shape and should not be touched.

The defects cluster almost entirely in narrative mechanism claims, and four of them are inversions — the skill states the opposite of the platform. The guest-user-security failure is the worst: it teaches "set OWD to Public Read Only, sharing rules can't help you" when the platform forces guest OWD to Private and makes guest sharing rules the only path, and one worked example recommends Public Read/Write on Case for an unauthenticated site. Two other inversions (Spring '22 "added" guest permission-set assignment when it restricted it; "bind variables unavailable in dynamic strings") follow the same shape. Notably, three of these appear inside references/llm-anti-patterns.md files, where a wrong "correct pattern" doesn't just mislead — it trains a consuming model to reject the right answer. The Account__Share block is the sharpest example: the anti-pattern's stated wrong answer uses the real object name and its correct answer uses a fabricated one.

The single most useful structural signal is that this slice contradicts itself, and in each case one side is right: guest-user-security-audit states the guest sharing model correctly while guest-user-security inverts it; xss-and-injection-prevention gets bind variables right while secure-coding-review-checklist gets them wrong. Cross-skill contradiction within a domain is a cheap, high-yield detector — worth running before the next expensive verification pass.

There is also evidence the repair process works when applied: session-high-assurance-policies documents its own prior fabrication (UserInfo.getSessionSecurityLevel()), now carries it as the negative example, and every signature I checked in it is exact.

Two cautions for whoever fixes this. First, do not treat "View Encrypted Data" and the session minimum-wins claim as equivalent: the former is wrong with high confidence, the latter I could not settle and have marked UNVERIFIABLE — the only official text says profile settings "override" org-wide settings with no direction specified, so it needs an org test, not an edit. Second, help.salesforce.com does not render for WebFetch under its normal /s/articleView URLs; the /apex/HTViewHelpDoc?id=<doc>.htm form works for many topics and is what most of these verifications ran through. The next agent will waste an hour rediscovering that.
retired: Connected Apps as the default integration surface — 413 lines across skills/security treat 'Connected App' as the current product for OAuth/JWT/client-credentials integrations, and only 3 lines (all in connected-app-security-policies) mention External Client Apps. Salesforce now blocks new connected-app creation by default in new orgs and directs new integrations to External Client Apps. Skills such as api-security-and-rate-limiting, oauth-token-management, service-account-credential-rotation and mfa-enforcement-patterns give Setup paths (App Manager > Connected App > OAuth Policies / Session Policies) that a practitioner in a Spring '26 org may not be able to follow for a NEW app. Not a fabrication — the guidance is right for existing apps — but the whole slice needs an External Client Apps overlay.

confirmed_fabrications.why_wrong: Crypto.generateMac supports exactly four algorithm names: hmacMD5, hmacSHA1, hmacSHA256, hmacSHA512. HmacSHA384 is not one of them. security_severity.claim: Supported algorithms are `HmacSHA1`, `HmacSHA256`, `HmacSHA384`, `HmacSHA512`, and the weaker `HmacMD5`
security_severity.why_wrong: Crypto.generateMac supports exactly four algorithm names: hmacMD5, hmacSHA1, hmacSHA256, hmacSHA512. HmacSHA384 is not one of them. A developer following this skill to match a vendor that signs with HMAC-SHA384 would write Crypto.generateMac('HmacSHA384', ...) and get a runtime exception — in a webhook signature-verification path, i.e. the security control fails closed at best and gets 'fixed' by removing verification at worst. Crypto.sign/signWithCertificate DO support RSA-SHA384 and ECDSA-SHA384, which is probably where the confusion came from.
security_severity.correct_value: generateMac: hmacMD5, hmacSHA1, hmacSHA256, hmacSHA512 only. For SHA-384 HMAC there is no native Apex support.

security_severity.claim: Since Spring '21, guest sharing rules cannot grant access to Private OWD records. The only way to give guest users access to records is to set the OWD to Public Read Only. Use Apex filtering to control which of those public records the guest actually sees.

Secure Guest User Record Access forces a separate guest-user org-wide default of Private for ALL objects, and the official page states 'This access level can't be changed.' Guest user sharing rules are the ONLY mechanism that grants guest record access, and they are capped at Read Only. The skill tells practitioners to do the one thing the platform no longer permits (set guest OWD to Public) and to abandon the one mechanism that actually works. The same skill's Common Patterns section (SKILL.md:132), Decision Guidance (SKILL.md:146), gotchas.md:39, well-architected.md:10 and examples.md:43 ('Set Case OWD to Public Read/Write') all repeat it. examples.md:43 is actively dangerous: it recommends Public Read/Write OWD on Case for an unauthenticated site.
